claims.text: A controlled intermediate-temperature hold during heating enhances atomic interdiffusion in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The intermediate-temperature hold produces more synchronized nucleation.
Enhanced interdiffusion and synchronized nucleation promote a homogeneous single-phase solid solution rather than phase-separated or segregated structures.
Rapid heating and cooling of equiatomic Au–Pd–Pt–Ag–Rh nanoparticles typically causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed intervention is a slower temperature ramp followed by a hold at 300–400 °C before reaching the final synthesis temperature and applying controlled cooling.
Atomic rearrangement occurs during the intermediate-temperature hold.
The noble-metal constituents have differential atomic mobilities under the proposed synthesis conditions.
An intermediate hold compensates for differential atomic mobilities among the noble metals.
The hold reduces premature nucleation and phase separation by allowing additional diffusion and equilibration.
Additional diffusion and equilibration align crystallization energies and nucleation timescales.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, the intermediate hold will produce a predominantly single-phase solid solution with reduced secondary-phase signals.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, the intermediate hold will produce more uniform particle morphology and elemental distributions.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to solution-phase noble-metal high-entropy alloy systems such as Au–Pd–Pt–Ag–Rh under rapid-heating regimes.
The intervention's effectiveness may depend on composition, heating rate, hold temperature, and hold duration.

contradictions.description: The explicit Au–Pd–Pt–Ag–Rh system contains exactly five elements, whereas the task regime specifies nanoparticles containing more than five elements. Thus, the stated exemplar falls outside the requested compositional boundary.
